lead: A gyroscope is a rotor spinning fast about its axis. Left alone, the spin axis keeps pointing the same way in space, however the aircraft turns around it: that is rigidity. Push on the axis and it does not move the way you pushed; it turns at right angles, and that motion is precession. Rigidity gives the attitude and heading indicators a fixed reference, and precession against a spring gives the turn indicator its rate. This chapter works out both from H = Iω and covers nutation, TDF and SDF gyros, drift and the cockpit gyro instruments.
prereq: You need torque, moment of inertia and angular velocity from basic mechanics, and the frames of geometric concepts of navigation. The autopilot that uses gyro signals is in Autopilot and automatic flight control.

sections.h3: Rigidity, gimbals and degrees of freedom

blocks.text: A rotor spinning about its axis carries angular momentum H, a vector along the spin axis. With no external torque, H stays fixed in inertial space. That is rigidity in space. More mass far from the axis, or a faster spin, raises H and so rigidity.

blocks.where: H is angular momentum in kg·m²/s; I is the rotor's moment of inertia about its spin axis in kg·m²; ω is the spin rate in rad/s (rpm × 2π ÷ 60).

blocks.text: The rotor sits in gimbals: rings pivoted on bearings so that the case can turn without twisting the rotor. A rotor in two gimbals is free about both axes at right angles to its spin: it is a free gyro, or two-degree-of-freedom (TDF) gyro. (Some books also count the spin and say "three planes of freedom"; it is the same gyro.) A rotor in one gimbal can turn about one axis only: a single-degree-of-freedom (SDF) gyro. TDF gyros measure angles (attitude, heading); SDF gyros, restrained by a spring or a damper, measure rates.

If two gimbal axes line up, one freedom is lost and the gyro cannot follow a turn about the missing axis: gimbal lock. Caging locks the gimbals (not the rotor, which keeps spinning) to hold the axis square to the case before start or in aerobatics. Erection brings a vertical gyro's axis back to the local vertical slowly, with pendulous air vanes or small torque motors.

A torque changes angular momentum: T = dH/dt. The change dH points along the torque vector T, not along the push. When T is at right angles to H, the length of H does not change; only its direction does, and the tip of H moves towards T.
Ω = T ÷ H = T ÷ (I ω)    (T at right angles to H)
blocks.where: Ω is the steady precession rate in rad/s; T is the torque component at right angles to the spin axis in N·m; H = Iω. A torque along the spin axis only speeds the rotor up or slows it down.

blocks.text: A practical rule gives the direction: picture the force applied at the rim of the rotor, then carry that point 90° round in the direction of spin. The rotor moves as if pushed there. A big H makes Ω small, which is why instrument rotors spin at 20 000 rpm and more.

sections.h3: Nutation, drift and the rate gyro

blocks.text: Apply a torque suddenly and the axis overshoots, tracing small fast loops around the steady precession path: nutation. For a symmetric rotor the loops repeat at about ωn = H ÷ It, where It is the moment of inertia about a gimbal axis; a fast rotor nutates fast and in tiny circles. Friction and damping in the gimbal bearings remove it, leaving pure precession.

Drift is any unwanted wandering of the spin axis. Real drift comes from torques the gyro should not feel: bearing friction, imbalance, gimbal friction. Apparent drift is not a motion of the gyro at all; the Earth turns beneath an axis that stays fixed in space. For a directional gyro, the apparent drift about the local vertical is 15.04 × sin φ °/h at latitude φ: 15.04 °/h at a pole, zero at the equator. Flying east or west adds transport wander, because the local north turns as longitude changes.

A rate gyro is an SDF gyro whose gimbal is held by a spring of stiffness k. When the case turns at rate Ω about the input axis, the gyro needs a torque HΩ to turn with it; the gimbal tilts until the spring supplies that torque. So the steady deflection measures the rate. With a viscous damper in place of the spring the deflection measures the integral of rate, which is angle: a rate-integrating gyro.

blocks.where: θ is the gimbal deflection in rad; H is the rotor's angular momentum; Ω is the turn rate about the input axis in rad/s; k is the spring stiffness in N·m/rad.

blocks.text: Ring laser and fibre-optic gyros replace the spinning mass with light travelling round a closed path; they are covered in inertial sensors and inertial navigation systems.

examples.question: A directional gyro rotor has I = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² and spins at 24 000 rpm. Bearing friction applies a torque of 5 × 10⁻⁶ N·m at right angles to the spin axis. (a) Find H. (b) Find the real drift rate in °/h. (c) At Chennai (13° N) add the apparent drift in the same sense, and find the heading error after 15 minutes.
steps: In degrees per hour: 1.6579 × 10⁻⁵ × (180 ÷ π) × 3600 = 3.42 °/h of real drift.
Total = 3.42 + 3.38 = 6.80 °/h; in 15 minutes the card is off by 6.80 × 0.25 = 1.7°.
examples.answer: H = 0.302 kg·m²/s; real drift 3.42 °/h; with 3.38 °/h apparent drift the heading is about 1.7° wrong after 15 minutes, which is why the heading indicator is reset to the compass regularly.

examples.question: A turn indicator's rate gyro has I = 5 × 10⁻⁵ kg·m² and spins at 12 000 rpm; its spring stiffness is k = 0.04 N·m/rad. (a) Find the gimbal deflection in a rate-one turn (3°/s). (b) What turn rate gives a 10° deflection?
steps: Rate one: Ω = 3°/s = 0.05236 rad/s. Gyroscopic torque HΩ = 0.06283 × 0.05236 = 3.290 × 10⁻³ N·m.
examples.answer: A rate-one turn deflects the gimbal 4.71°; a 10° deflection means 6.37 °/s, a little over rate two. Deflection is proportional to rate, so the scale is linear.

traps: Precession is at right angles to the push: carry the push 90° round in the direction of spin. Drawing the axis moving along the push loses the marks.
Convert rpm to rad/s before Ω = T/(Iω). Using rpm directly makes Ω come out 9.55 times too small (the wrong answer is the right one × 2π/60).
Nutation is a short transient after a sudden torque; precession is the steady motion. Do not swap them.
Apparent drift is the Earth turning under a fixed axis; real drift is from friction and imbalance. Only real drift is cured by a better gyro.
A turn coordinator shows rate of turn, not bank angle; it is an SDF rate gyro, not a vertical gyro.

quiz.a: With no external torque, the spin axis of a gyro keeps a fixed direction in inertial space, because its angular momentum H = Iω stays constant.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a TDF and an SDF gyro?
quiz.a: A TDF (free) gyro has two gimbals and is free about both axes at right angles to its spin; it measures angles. An SDF gyro has one gimbal, is free about one axis only, and with a spring or damper measures rate or integrated rate.

quiz.q: Why does a rate gyro need a spring while an attitude gyro must not have one?
quiz.a: A rate gyro measures the torque needed to turn H with the case; the spring supplies it and its deflection shows the rate. An attitude gyro must hold its axis fixed in space, and any spring would drag the axis round with the aircraft.

quiz.q: A rotor has I = 0.05 kg·m² and spins at 12 000 rpm. A steady torque of 0.02 N·m acts at right angles to the spin axis. Find Ω in degrees per minute.
The rotor of the first worked example has I<sub>t</sub> = 0.8 × 10⁻⁴ kg·m² about its gimbal axis. Estimate its nutation frequency and say why it is rarely noticed.
quiz.a: ω<sub>n</sub> = H ÷ I<sub>t</sub> = 0.3016 ÷ 0.8 × 10⁻⁴ = 3770 rad/s, about 600 Hz. Loops that fast are tiny in size and the gimbal friction damps them in a moment, so the needle shows only steady precession.

quiz.q: Why must a heading indicator be reset to the magnetic compass, while a turn coordinator never needs a reset?
quiz.a: The heading indicator is a free gyro holding a direction in space; real and apparent drift add up to several degrees per hour, and it has no sense of north. The turn coordinator measures a rate against a spring: when the turn stops, the spring returns the gimbal to zero, so there is nothing to accumulate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Spinning-mass gyros are giving way to optical and MEMS gyros with no bearings to wear. Search for dynamically tuned gyro, Sagnac effect and MEMS Coriolis gyroscope.

Right, a vector diagram: H of 0.3016 kilogram metre squared per second points right, the friction torque of 5 micronewton metres points up at right angles, the small change dH equals T times dt, and H a moment later is turned slightly towards T. A box gives omega equals T over H, 1.66 times ten to the minus five radians per second, or 3.42 degrees per hour of real drift, plus 3.38 degrees per hour of apparent drift at 13 degrees north.
